query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment forming a thin, adherent α‑Al2O3 scale on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA bond coats enhances long-term durability by serving as a protective barrier during subsequent high-temperature operation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA bond coat without any prior oxidation treatment.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-deposited bond coat to a pre-oxidation heat treatment at 900 °C in air for 1–2 hours to deliberately form a thin, continuous α‑Al2O3 layer.
generation.conditions: Subsequent exposure to 900 °C during service, including corrosive environments with molten salts.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a seeded, adherent α‑Al2O3 thermally grown oxide that minimizes further oxidation and reduces thermal stress at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide scale serves as a barrier to oxygen diffusion and helps maintain the integrity of the bond coat by reducing the thermal mismatch during cyclic operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in additional oxide spallation by approximately 40% and a more stable TGO structure compared to coatings without pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.baseline: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA bond coat without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Effective provided that the pre-oxidation does not generate a scale too thick to induce excessive stresses; optimum at controlled scale thickness (<1 μm).
generation.uncertainty: Risk of over-oxidation or scale delamination if the pre-oxidation parameters are not precisely controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two groups of bond coats: one group subjected to the controlled pre-oxidation treatment (900 °C, 1–2 hours in air) and a second group kept as-deposited. Expose both groups to cyclic 900 °C thermal corrosion tests in molten salt environments.
measurements: Examination of TGO thickness and integrity via cross-sectional SEM.
Quantification of further oxide spallation area after cyclic testing.
Adhesion testing of the bond coats post-treatment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate at least a 40% reduction in additional spallation and maintain better TGO integrity compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:6. Maps for Bond Coat Alloys
cited_evidence.text: Most likely, an EC for use with metallic UHTMs will consist of metallic bond coat (BC)/thermally grown oxide (TGO)/top coat (TC) []; in other words, the EC could be of the BC/TGO/TC type []. The EC must also provide protection against contamination by CMAS (CaO-MgO-Al2O3-SiO2). A prerequisite for the substrate alloy is to have adequate oxidation allied with the oxidation goal, and for the BC to be compatible with the substrate. It is desirable for the BC to form an adhering αAl2O3 scale as the TGO. Furthermore, the BC could consist of layers of different materials because it must also shield the substrate from interstitial contamination [,]. RM(Nb)ICs and RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs cannot form αAl2O3 scales [,]. The same seems to be the case for the other RCCAs studied to date [].

Metallic ultrahigh-temperature materials (UHTMs) (i.e., RM(Nb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, PM(Nb)ICs/RHEAs, and RHEAs and RCCAs with Nb and Si addition) and the alloying behaviour and properties of alloys and their phases were considered by using maps of the parameters δ, Δχ, and VEC, which are indispensable in the alloy-design methodology NICE. What connects and what differentiates the material groups was discussed by using parameter maps. Attention was drawn to the fact that high-entropy or complex concentrated intermetallics, namely 5-3 silicides, C14 Laves and A15 compounds, and bcc solid solutions and eutectics can form in metallic UHTMs where such phases co-exist with conventional phases. The practicality of maps for the design/selection of substrate alloys with different properties was deliberated. The need for environmental coatings for metallic UHTMs was considered, and the design of bond coat alloys was discussed by using relevant maps.

papers.title: Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy coatings, with and without Y and Hf co-doping
papers.approach: Laser cladding to produce both conventional EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings; followed by heat treatment at 900 °C and hot corrosion tests under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts.
papers.findings: The coatings exhibited mixed FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase precipitated; grain growth was less pronounced in the YHf co-doped coating. Under hot corrosion, differences in oxide scale spallation were observed—with indications that reactive element co-doping can improve resistance to scale spallation.
papers.mechanism: The incorporation of reactive elements (Y and Hf) allegedly slows diffusion and stabilizes the microstructure via solute drag, which helps form a more adherent oxide scale by reducing grain boundary mobility and hindering oxidation-related failure.

papers.title: Preparation of VZrHfNbTa High-Entropy Alloy-Based High-Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Coating and Its Bonding Mechanism.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy-based coatings on substrates using VZrHfNbTa compositions with a Hf-rich outer layer
papers.approach: Hot-press sintering with a carbon environment to produce an HfC-rich surface and a gradient HfZr interlayer that bonds to the substrate.
papers.findings: The formation of a thin (<10 μm) HfC layer and a gradient HfZr alloy at the interface improved adhesion. Enhanced oxidation tests showed that the coated sample gained significantly less weight due to the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer.
papers.mechanism: Diffusive migration of zirconium and reactive interaction between Hf and carbon (forming HfC) produce a gradient composite layer. This gradient enhances the bonding between the coating and substrate and improves oxidation resistance by forming a durable oxide scale.

papers.title: Significantly Improving the High-Temperature Tensile Properties of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1 Alloys b
papers.system: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys based on Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1 with trace Hf additions
papers.approach: Alloying with incremental amounts of Hf (from 0 up to 0.8 at%) and mechanical testing at room temperature and 700 °C to assess the effect on tensile properties
papers.findings: Trace Hf additions led to the precipitation of Hf-rich phases at interfaces, which significantly improved the high-temperature strength and ductility (optimal at 0.5 at% Hf), while room temperature properties remained almost unchanged.
papers.mechanism: The Hf-rich phases act as barriers to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, resulting in improved high-temperature deformation behavior. The precipitation acts as an interface strengthener without altering the major phase morphology.

papers.title: Refractory Metal Intermetallic Composites, High-Entropy Alloys, and Complex Concentrated Alloys: A Route to Selecting Substrate Alloys and Bond Coat A
papers.system: Metallic ultrahigh-temperature materials and associated bond coats
papers.approach: Mapping alloy design parameters (δ, Δχ, VEC) for selecting substrate and bond coat materials, with an emphasis on ensuring compatibility to form an adherent α-Al2O3 scale
papers.findings: Bond coats with composition tuned to promote the formation of a stable, adherent aluminum oxide scale may protect substrates from interstitial contamination and oxidation failure. The discussion highlights the importance of reactive elements and intermetallic phases in high-temperature environments.
papers.mechanism: Optimized chemical composition promotes the formation of a protective, adherent α-Al2O3 scale (TGO), while controlling interdiffusion between the bond coat and substrate.

papers.title: Optimization of Process Parameters for Laser-Directed Energy Deposition Coatings of FeCoNi + 1%Y2O3 High-Entropy Alloy Based on ...
papers.system: FeCoNi based high-entropy alloy coatings with 1% Y2O3 addition
papers.approach: Laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) with optimized process parameters to incorporate Y2O3 for microstructure refinement and improved interfacial bonding
papers.findings: The introduction of Y2O3 led to a refined microstructure, improved hardness, and enhanced interfacial bonding through the formation of oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) phases. These coatings demonstrated stable FCC phases and an average microhardness around 167 HV.
papers.mechanism: Y2O3 particles serve as effective grain refiners and oxygen scavengers. Their dispersion contributes to oxide dispersion strengthening, which increases the mechanical stability and oxidation resistance of the coating.

established: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit superior thermal stability and oxidation resistance due to sluggish diffusion kinetics.
Reactive element additions (such as Y, Hf, or rare earth oxides) can improve oxidation resistance and scale adherence in high-temperature environments.
Good bonding in bond coat systems requires the formation of a gradient or interlayer that promotes an adherent, protective thermally grown oxide (TGO), preferably α-Al2O3.

approaches_tried.approach: Y and Hf co-doping in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 coatings via laser cladding
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced thermal stability and a modified oxide scale spallation behavior under hot corrosion conditions at 900 °C; challenges remain in quantifying optimal spallation reduction.

approaches_tried.approach: Hot-press sintering to apply a Hf-rich coating with gradient Zr diffusion
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of a gradient interlayer (HfC and HfZr alloy) that improves interfacial bonding and reduces oxidation in extreme environments.

approaches_tried.approach: Trace Hf addition to dual-phase HEAs for mechanical property improvement at high temperatures
approaches_tried.outcome: Significantly enhanced high-temperature tensile properties (strength and ductility) with minimal adverse effects at room temperature.

approaches_tried.approach: Incorporation of 1% Y2O3 in FeCoNi-based HEA coatings via LDED
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved microstructure refinement, hardness uniformity, and interfacial bonding, leading to enhanced high-temperature performance.

mechanisms: Reactive element effect: Reactive elements (e.g., Hf, Y) reduce grain boundary mobility and hinder diffusion, stabilizing the microstructure and improving oxide scale adhesion.
Formation of gradient interlayers: Designing diffusion gradients (e.g., via Zr migration) improves mechanical bonding between coating and substrate.
Oxide dispersion strengthening: Incorporation of fine oxide particles (e.g., Y2O3) refines grains and acts as obstacles to dislocation motion.
disagreements: Some reports show conflicting quantitative outcomes regarding the extent of scale spallation reduction when using Y and Hf co-doping, indicating that microstructural effects may vary with processing parameters.

Variability exists in the reported influence of reactive element additions on phase stability versus mechanical enhancement; in some systems, the impact on microstructure is minimal while in others, precipitate formation is significant.
open_questions: What is the optimal reactive element (or combination) and dosing level (e.g., Hf alone versus Hf with Y) to most effectively improve bond coat durability while maintaining desirable mechanical properties?
How do these interventions perform under prolonged thermal cycling and exposure to CMAS or other aggressive environments typical of TBC systems?
What are the long-term interface evolution mechanisms between the HEA bond coat and the thermally grown oxide (TGO) during service?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of trace Hf addition as a single intervention in HEA bond coats to promote the formation of a stable, adherent α-Al2O3 TGO, thereby improving durability and reliability.
Explore combining reactive element doping with oxide dispersion strategies (e.g., Y2O3) in a controlled manner to synergistically enhance both mechanical and oxidation resistance properties.

Perform systematic high-temperature cyclic oxidation and CMAS infiltration experiments to establish clear performance benchmarks and identify conditions under which the intervention remains effective.

directions.direction: Incorporate trace reactive element Hf into the HEA bond coat during deposition.
directions.assessment: Directly targets durability by stabilizing microstructure; mechanism supported by known reactive element effects (solute drag, grain boundary pinning) as evidenced in literature (PMC10488378, PMC10647333). Feasible using laser cladding with controlled Hf additions.

directions.direction: Introduce a minor content of Y2O3 into the HEA bond coat via powder modification.
directions.assessment: Addresses durability via grain refinement and oxygen-scavenging to form ODS phases, which are known to improve oxidation resistance at high temperatures. Prior evidence (PMC11857518) supports this approach, and process control appears manageable.

directions.direction: Apply a post-deposition ultrasonic burnishing (UB) treatment to the HEA bond coat.
directions.assessment: Directly improves surface grain refinement and introduces beneficial compressive stresses that enhance interface adhesion. Well supported by UB-induced grain refinement literature (PMC9416578); relatively straightforward to implement after deposition.

directions.direction: Pre-oxidize the as-deposited HEA bond coat to form a thin, adherent α‑Al2O3 scale prior to service.
directions.assessment: This intervention forms an initial protective TGO that can mitigate further oxidation and spallation during high-temperature exposure. It leverages established TBC strategies (PMC9028980) and is a single-step thermal process, though care must be taken to control scale thickness.

candidates.hypothesis: Trace Hf doping in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA bond coats improves high-temperature durability by stabilizing the microstructure via reactive element effects.
candidates.intervention: Addition of 0.5 at.% Hf to the feedstock during laser cladding.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporation of 1 wt% Y2O3 into FeCoNi-based HEA bond coats improves coating durability by forming a stable oxide dispersion that refines the microstructure and enhances TGO adherence.
candidates.intervention: Modification of the feedstock to include 1 wt% Y2O3 during the LDED process.

candidates.hypothesis: Post-deposition ultrasonic burnishing (UB) treatment of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA bond coats refines the surface grain structure, leading to reduced cracking and enhanced bonding durability.
candidates.intervention: Application of ultrasonic burnishing with a defined pressure (e.g., 50 N) and multiple passes (e.g., three passes) on the as-deposited coating.

minor_issues: Potential challenges in achieving uniform dispersion of Y2O3 in the HEA matrix under LDED conditions.
Limited discussion of possible trade-offs, such as ductility loss or unwanted secondary phases.
fixes: Provide additional LDED parameter optimization data to ensure consistent Y2O3 distribution.
Include mechanical and microstructural characterization at different service temperatures and times to confirm stability.
evidence_needs: Further reports or datasets quantifying the influence of small additions of Y2O3 on FeCoNi-based alloys under thermal cycling and corrosive environments.
Long-term exposure data for coated systems to confirm scale adhesion and mechanical performance over multiple cycles.

minor_issues: Unclear whether UB-induced compressive stresses remain during prolonged high-temperature service.
Risk of microcrack formation if UB parameters (pressure, passes) are not optimized.
fixes: Evaluate residual stress after repeated thermal cycles to confirm retention of beneficial compressive stress.
Clarify UB process parameters (e.g., rolling speed, amplitude, tool geometry) and how they scale for industrial use.
evidence_needs: Comparative studies on UB-treated high-entropy coatings under thermal cycling to validate longevity of mechanical improvements.

Potential variability in α-Al2O3 growth kinetics depending on alloy composition and furnace atmosphere.
fixes: Optimize pre-oxidation protocols (time, temperature, atmosphere) to achieve uniform, thin α-Al2O3 scales.
Monitor scale microstructure and bonding at intermediate intervals during cyclic testing.

Mechanical and microstructural evaluations of pre-oxidized coatings after multiple thermal cycles with salt exposure.

fixes: Characterize the Hf-rich phases more thoroughly (e.g., composition, morphology, distribution) during and after high-temperature exposure.
Include multiple Hf concentration levels to determine an optimal dosing window.

Long-duration corrosion-fatigue studies to confirm the stability of the microstructure and TGO adherence.
